steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for my paper on popular, perfect and Pareto-optimal matchings in one-sided matching markets (house allocation) with capacities, including what happens when we are allowed to modify the house capacities. Include the setting, the optimality notions, our contributions, related work and the paper structure.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Setting: matching markets with one-sided preferences (house allocation)
2. What makes a good matching: perfectness, Pareto-optimality, popularity
3. Our contributions
4. Related work
5. Paper structure

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Setting
- two-sided markets, one-sided preferences: house allocation, school choice, more
- allocate set H of heterogeneous indivisible goods among set A of agents / assign applicants A to houses/jobs H
- strict preferences over acceptable goods/houses = house allocation (ha) problem
- widely studied; now also used to model kidney exchange programs
- other uses: students to schools, graduates to trainee positions, professors to offices, clients to servers
- one or both sides may have capacities; terminology: applicants vs houses
- goal: good assignment between A and H without violating capacities

2. Good matchings
- perfect: every applicant matched (saturated if capacities); important in school choice
- Pareto-optimal: no other allocation where all applicants better off; most mechanisms aim for it
- popular: no M^{\prime} that beats M head to head (more agents prefer M^{\prime} to M than vice versa)
- unit capacities: comparison straightforward; otherwise definition varies
- we use the traditional definition (prior work) and a lexicographic one (other prior work)
- popular => Pareto-optimal (a dominating M^{\prime} wins under any natural definition)
- but Pareto-optimal / popular need not be perfect

3. Contributions
- applicants with capacities: even finding a popular matching NP-hard; answers open question from prior work
- holds for applicant capacities at most 3 (traditional), at most 2 (lexicographic)
- so main focus: only houses have capacities
- optimally modify house capacities -> perfect + Pareto-optimal, or perfect + popular matching
- two criteria: Min Sum and Min Max of capacity changes
- Pareto case easy: maximum size Pareto-optimal matchings always exist, trivial lower bound tight
- popularity, increase only, Min Sum: polynomial-time
- increase and decrease (decreasing can help, examples): NP-hard
- Min Max: both versions NP-hard, hard to approximate within a constant factor
- contrast: two-sided preferences, stable / (one-sided)-popular: Min Max solvable, Min Sum NP-hard (prior work)

4. Related work
- popular matching introduced for unit capacities, two-sided preferences; later extended to many-to-many
- house allocation: unit capacities first, then arbitrary house capacities; open question about non-unit capacities on the preference side
- partly solved, only for preferences with ties; same work: lexicographic many-to-one popularity
- capacity changes for optimal allocation studied a lot, mostly two-sided preferences
- closest work: optimally increasing capacities for several criteria at once, two-sided, always stability; ours = one-sided
- further capacity variation papers: seat costs to assign all students; seat-extension mechanism for welfare; strategy-proof mechanism for min/max quotas; couples, stable matching by perturbing capacities; AvgRank / CarSM; alternative method + experiments for Min Sum AvgRank; fixed resources determining school capacities

5. Paper structure
- Section 2: concepts, definitions
- Section 3: NP-hardness of popular matching existence with agent capacities
- Section 4: only houses have capacities; perturb capacities as little as possible
- perfect + popular: algorithm for Min Sum, NP-hard for Min Max
- Pareto + perfect: simple solution to both

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Two-sided matching markets where only one side has preferences come up in many applications, such as house allocation, school choice and more. These problems often correspond to allocating a set H of heterogeneous indivisible goods among a set A of agents, or to assigning a set A of applicants to a set H of houses/jobs. The agents/applicants are assumed to have some strict preferences over the goods/houses that they find acceptable. This is called the house allocation (ha) problem. The house allocation problem is widely studied in the literature, especially nowadays, since it has started to be used to model kidney exchange programs too.

These frameworks are also used for allocating students to schools, graduates to trainee positions, professors to offices, clients to servers, etc. In many of these applications one side of the market or both sides can have capacities. To unify terminology and follow the literature, we call one side of the market the applicants and the other side the houses. Our goal is to find a good assignment between A and H that does not violate the capacity constraints.

What counts as a good matching depends on the application. The simplest concept is that every applicant is matched (or saturated if they have capacities), and we call such allocations perfect. Having a perfect allocation is particularly important in school choice, since every student should be admitted to some school. Another widely used concept is Pareto-optimality. An allocation is Pareto-optimal if there is no other allocation where all of the applicants are better off. Pareto-optimality is of course a very desirable concept and most mechanisms aim to satisfy it.

Finally, another well known and studied concept is popularity. A matching M is popular if there is no other matching M^{\prime} such that M would lose in a head to head comparison with M^{\prime}, i.e. more agents would prefer M^{\prime} to M than the other way around. If the applicants have unit capacities, comparing two allocations is straightforward, but otherwise the concept of popularity can vary by definition. In this paper we consider both the traditional version of the definition and another natural one which compares two allocations in a lexicographic way.

It is not hard to see that if an assignment M is popular, it also has to be Pareto-optimal. Clearly a matching M^{\prime} where each applicant (weakly) improves and at least one strictly improves dominates M with respect to any natural definition. However, a Pareto-optimal or a popular matching need not be perfect.

Our contributions.
- applicants with capacities: even finding a popular matching NP-hard; answers open question from prior work
- holds for applicant capacities at most 3 (traditional), at most 2 (lexicographic)
- so main focus: only houses have capacities
- optimally modify house capacities -> perfect + Pareto-optimal, or perfect + popular matching
- two criteria: Min Sum and Min Max of capacity changes
- Pareto case easy: maximum size Pareto-optimal matchings always exist, trivial lower bound tight
- popularity, increase only, Min Sum: polynomial-time; increase and decrease (decreasing can help, examples): NP-hard
- Min Max: both versions NP-hard, hard to approximate within a constant factor
- contrast: two-sided preferences, stable / (one-sided)-popular: Min Max solvable, Min Sum NP-hard (prior work)

Related work.
- popular matching introduced for unit capacities, two-sided preferences; later extended to many-to-many
- house allocation: unit capacities first, then arbitrary house capacities; open question about non-unit capacities on the preference side
- partly solved, only for preferences with ties; same work: lexicographic many-to-one popularity
- capacity changes for optimal allocation studied a lot, mostly two-sided preferences
- closest work: optimally increasing capacities for several criteria at once, two-sided, always stability; ours = one-sided
- further capacity variation papers: seat costs; seat-extension mechanism; strategy-proof min/max quotas; couples; AvgRank / CarSM; Min Sum AvgRank experiments; fixed resources

Paper structure.
- Section 2: concepts, definitions; Section 3: NP-hardness with agent capacities
- Section 4: only houses have capacities; perturb capacities as little as possible
- perfect + popular: algorithm for Min Sum, NP-hard for Min Max; Pareto + perfect: simple solution to both

steps.text:
Two-sided matching markets where only one side has preferences come up in many applications, such as house allocation, school choice and more. These problems often correspond to allocating a set H of heterogeneous indivisible goods among a set A of agents, or to assigning a set A of applicants to a set H of houses/jobs. The agents/applicants are assumed to have some strict preferences over the goods/houses that they find acceptable. This is called the house allocation (ha) problem. The house allocation problem is widely studied in the literature, especially nowadays, since it has started to be used to model kidney exchange programs too.

These frameworks are also used for allocating students to schools, graduates to trainee positions, professors to offices, clients to servers, etc. In many of these applications one side of the market or both sides can have capacities. To unify terminology and follow the literature, we call one side of the market the applicants and the other side the houses. Our goal is to find a good assignment between A and H that does not violate the capacity constraints.

What counts as a good matching depends on the application. The simplest concept is that every applicant is matched (or saturated if they have capacities), and we call such allocations perfect. Having a perfect allocation is particularly important in school choice, since every student should be admitted to some school. Another widely used concept is Pareto-optimality. An allocation is Pareto-optimal if there is no other allocation where all of the applicants are better off. Pareto-optimality is of course a very desirable concept and most mechanisms aim to satisfy it.

Finally, another well known and studied concept is popularity. A matching M is popular if there is no other matching M^{\prime} such that M would lose in a head to head comparison with M^{\prime}, i.e. more agents would prefer M^{\prime} to M than the other way around. If the applicants have unit capacities, comparing two allocations is straightforward, but otherwise the concept of popularity can vary by definition. In this paper we consider both the traditional version of the definition and another natural one which compares two allocations in a lexicographic way.

It is not hard to see that if an assignment M is popular, it also has to be Pareto-optimal. Clearly a matching M^{\prime} where each applicant (weakly) improves and at least one strictly improves dominates M with respect to any natural definition. However, a Pareto-optimal or a popular matching need not be perfect.

Our contributions.

If the applicants can have capacities, we show that even finding a popular matching is NP-hard, which answers an open question from earlier work. This is true even if the capacities of the applicants are at most 3 in the traditional version and at most 2 in the lexicographic one. Therefore we mainly focus on the version where only the houses can have capacities.

We study how to optimally modify the capacities of the houses so that the resulting instance admits a perfect and Pareto optimal matching, or a perfect and popular matching. We consider two optimality criteria: minimizing the sum of the capacity changes, and minimizing the maximum of the capacity changes. The Pareto-optimality case is rather easy, because there are always maximum size Pareto-optimal matchings, so the trivial lower bound, the minimum number of applicants who are not matched in an allocation, is tight. For popularity we get some nice and surprising results. If we can only increase the capacities, minimizing the sum of changes can be solved in polynomial time. But if we can also decrease the capacities (which can be beneficial in some cases, as we will show on some examples), the problem becomes NP-hard. Surprisingly, if we minimize the maximum of the capacity changes, both versions are NP-hard and also hard to approximate within a constant factor. This is very different from recent results for two-sided preferences and stable and (one-sided)-popular matchings, where the Min Max case is solvable and the Min Sum case is NP-hard.

Related work.

The popular matching problem was first introduced for markets with unit capacities and two-sided preferences. Later popularity was extended to many-to-many instances.

Popularity has also been studied in the house allocation model, first with unit capacities, and then with arbitrary capacities on the houses, where it was also asked as an open question whether a popular matching can be found in polynomial time if the side with preferences has non-unit capacities. This question was partly solved by later work, but only for preferences that may contain ties. That work also defined an extension of popularity to many-to-one instances, where agents compare matchings lexicographically.

Achieving optimal allocations through capacity changes has been studied a lot in recent literature, but mostly for markets where both sides have preferences. The closest to our work is a recent paper which also studied how to optimally increase the capacities to get matchings satisfying multiple optimality criteria at the same time. They studied markets with two-sided preferences, where one of the optimality notions was always stability. Our work looks at similar problems for markets where only one side has preferences.

Other papers have also examined capacity variations. One paper studied student-school allocations where each seat at the schools has some cost, and the aim is to assign all students with minimum cost. Another proposes a seat-extension mechanism to increase student welfare. A strategy-proof mechanism for minimum and maximum quotas has also been designed. Many-to-one matching with couples has been studied too, with algorithms that find a stable matching by perturbing the capacities. Capacity variations have also been considered to get a stable matching with minimum sum of the ranks of the matched schools (AvgRank) or with maximum cardinality (CarSM). Some alternative method with experiments for Min Sum AvgRank has also been proposed. And the problem where there is a fixed number of resources and the capacities of the schools depend on how much resource is allocated to them has been considered as well.

Paper structure. We start with the main concepts and definitions in Section 2. In Section 3 we prove NP-hardness of deciding whether a popular matching exists if agents have capacities. In Section 4 we consider the case where only the houses have capacities. We look at problems where the goal is to guarantee that desired solutions exist by perturbing the capacities as little as possible. When we want a perfect and popular matching, we give an algorithm if the objective is minimizing the sum of changes and show NP-hardness if we want to minimize the maximum of the changes. For Pareto-optimality and perfectness we give a simple solution to both problems.

We study the question of how to optimally modify the capacities of the houses such that the resulting instance admits a perfect and Pareto optimal, or a perfect and popular matching. We consider two optimality criteria: one aiming to minimize the sum of the capacity changes and one aiming to minimize the maximum of the capacity changes. The case of Pareto-optimality is rather easy, as there are always maximum size Pareto-optimal matchings, so the trivial lower bound, which is the minimum number of applicants who are not matched in an allocation, is tight. For popularity we obtain some nice and surprising results. We show that if we are only allowed to increase the capacities, then minimizing the sum of changes is polynomial-time solvable. However, if we are allowed to decrease the capacities too (which in some cases can be beneficial, as we will illustrate on some examples), then the problem becomes NP-hard. Surprisingly, if the maximum of the capacity changes is minimized, then both versions become NP-hard and also hard to approximate within a constant factor. This is in sharp contrast with recent results for two-sided preferences and stable and (one-sided)-popular matchings, where the Min Max case is solvable and the Min Sum case is NP-hard [4].

Related work.

The popular matching problem was first introduced for markets with unit capacities and two-sided preferences by [5]. Popularity was later extended to many-to-many instances by [1].

Popularity has also been explored in the house allocation model, first with unit capacities [6], then with arbitrary capacities on the houses [3], where they also posed as an open question whether a popular matching can be found in polynomial time if the side with preferences has non-unit capacities. This question has been partly solved by [2], but only for preferences which may contain ties. She also defined an extension of popularity to many-to-one instances, where agents compare matchings in a lexicographic fashion.

Achieving optimal allocations by capacity changes has been studied a lot in recent literature, although mostly for markets where both sides have preferences. Closest to our work is [4], where they also studied how to optimally increase the capacities to obtain matchings that satisfy multiple optimality criteria simultaneously. They studied markets with two-sided preferences, where one optimality notion was always stability. Our work investigates similar problems for markets where only one side has preferences.

There are further papers examining capacity variations. [7] studied student-school allocations where each seat at the schools has some cost, and the aim is to assign all students while minimizing the cost. [8] propose a seat-extension mechanism to increase students' welfare. [9] design a strategy-proof mechanism to address minimum and maximum quotas. [10] study many-to-one matching with couples and propose algorithms to find a stable matching by perturbing the capacities. [11,12] consider capacity variations to obtain a stable matching with minimum sum of the ranks of the matched schools (AvgRank) or maximum cardinality (CarSM). [13] propose an alternative method and conduct experiments for Min Sum AvgRank. [14] considered the problem where there is a fixed number of resources and the capacities of the schools are based on how much resource we allocate to them.

Paper structure. We start by introducing the main concepts and definitions in Section 2. Then, in Section 3 we prove NP-hardness of deciding if a popular matching exists if agents have capacities. In Section 4 we consider the case when only the houses have capacities. We investigate problems where our goal is to guarantee the existence of desired solutions by perturbing the capacities as little as possible. In the case when we aim for a perfect and popular matching, we provide an algorithm if the objective is to minimize the sum of changes, and show NP-hardness if we want to minimize the maximum of the changes. For Pareto-optimality and perfectness, we give a simple solution to both problems.
